questions.title: Function Contracts
questions.direct_answer: The full contract: parameter types (optional ?:, defaults, rest ...args: T[]), return types (annotate PUBLIC/boundary functions; let inference work locally), generics (T connecting input to output — function first<T>(a: T[]): T; CONSTRAINTS: T extends { id: string } limits while enabling keyof/discriminated access; keyof T + T[K] for the typed-property pattern; T extends any when a decorative generic connects nothing — the anti-pattern), function TYPES (type Handler = (e: Event) => void — the callable shape, with parameter bivariance vs strictFunctionTypes), overloads (signatures for REAL input→output relationships: pick(a: string): X; pick(a: number): Y — one implementation; the union-parameter trap: one union signature beats fake overloads), and the special returns: void (return IGNORED — callbacks: allows returning anything; a void-returning function type can accept a value-returning implementation), never (never returns — throw/infinite loops; the exhaustiveness check: default: const _x: never = value).

Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    F[function contract] --> P[params: optional defaults rest]
    F --> G[generics: CONNECT positions]
    G --> C[constraint: T extends X — require + unlock]
    G --> KK[keyof T + T[K] — exact property types]
    F --> O[overloads: real input→output maps, ONE impl]
    F --> R[returns]
    R --> V[void — ignored: callbacks may return values]
    R --> U[undefined — returns possibly nothing]
    R --> N[never — does not return: exhaustiveness sentinel]
    DECO[decorative generic — connects nothing] --> ANTI[the anti-pattern]
    SW[switch default: never check] --> EXH[new variant = compile error]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Parameter comparison strictness (the variance story worth one layer): by default, method-syntax parameters are BIVARIANT (accepts either direction — a historical JS-compat choice); strictFunctionTypes makes function-TYPE parameters CONTRAVARIANT (sound — the (x: Animal) handler accepts where Dog is expected, not the reverse). That single flag is why method syntax in interfaces behaves differently than property-with-function-type syntax for assignability — the deep 'why did this type error' answer for callback contracts.

The inference-priority mechanics (why annotations still matter at boundaries): TS infers from arguments + contextual typing + return statements — but PUBLIC API surfaces (exported functions, libraries) should annotate returns explicitly: inference that drifts (a widened literal, an unexpected undefined from a path) becomes a BREAKING change for every consumer; an explicit return type is a compile-enforced contract. The satisfies operator complements it: satisfies Config CHECKS the object against a contract while PRESERVING the literal types (the const config = { mode: 'dev' } satisfies Config case — 'dev' stays narrow AND is validated — the modern alternative to annotating it away).

The higher-order patterns (the senior layer): builder/curried functions need explicit generics on each stage (the type flows: function curry<T, R>(fn: (a: T) => R): (a: T) => R); type-level programming with conditional types in the return (T extends string ? string[] : never — the pattern behind Awaited, ReturnType, Parameters — the utility-type family that SHIPS this machinery); template-literal types in constraints (T extends `${string}-${string}` — validated ID formats at compile time); and the generic-inference gotcha: defaults on type parameters (T = unknown) can mask missing inference — a debugging tool, not a habit. The through-line: every piece of the function contract exists to make a relationship CHECKABLE at compile time — the answer to 'why type functions at all'.
